Enough fuel. The flight is safe.
Just enough fuel. It may fail!
Not enough fuel. The ship will turn back.
Out of fuel! Turning back to Earth.
The ship came back. Take less cargo or add fuel, then try again.
First, fly the crew to the Moon.
Order sent to Earth! The ship starts on schedule. You can still cancel it before the start.
No contact with Earth now. Wait for the next comms window.
The ship is already flying. Change the next order.
Very sick. Can only rest in the med bay.
There is no place for this job yet.
Nobody with this job is waiting on Earth.
A replacement is already on the list.
The antenna has no power. No contact with Earth.
The supply ship is waiting: the order was not sent.
The supply ship took off from Earth.
Not enough fuel! The supply ship turned back. It comes {0} hours later.
The supply ship landed on the pad.
Science from samples and the lab
Small and fast, but its hold is tiny.
The all-rounder: a medium hold at a normal speed.
The biggest hold, but the rocket itself is heavy and flies slowly.
Why choose? A bigger rocket carries more, but it is heavy itself and flies longer. While it flies, the base waits.
Tap ? next to any cargo to learn what it is for.
A kit is heavier than plain materials, but robots start building it right after landing.
Fuel is heavy too! More cargo means more fuel.
Water from Earth is VERY heavy: one tank gives only a little. It is better to mine ice on the Moon. Take water only for emergencies!
Food is hard to make on the Moon, so it is the main thing ships bring. Hungry astronauts work slowly.
Air to breathe. The base makes oxygen from water (life support), so from Earth take only a little, for emergencies. The tank holds up to 100.
Medicine for sick astronauts. Space radiation can make people ill.
Metal and plastic parts. Robots build any module from them.
A home for the crew: beds, a kitchen and strong walls.
Turns sunlight into electricity. At the south pole the Sun stays low, so the panels stand tall.
Stores electricity for the time when the panels are in shadow.
Thick walls against solar storms. Hide the crew here when the Sun is angry.
A small hospital. The medic heals people here.
Talks to Earth. Without contact you can't order new supplies.
Scientists study Moon rocks here and earn science points.
The kit landed. Robots started building: {0}.
The kit for {0} was unpacked into building materials.
The crew bus has arrived. The astronauts are boarding the rocket...
The tower arm moves away. Ready!
The crew is on the way to the Moon!
Not enough fuel! The crew is safe: the capsule landed in the ocean. Repack the rocket and try again.
A rocket pushes hot gas down hard, so the rocket goes up.
Most of a rocket's weight at launch is fuel.
During launch astronauts feel 3 to 4 times heavier than usual.
The Moon is about 384,000 km away. Real astronauts flew there in about 3 days.
Too heavy! Add fuel, pick a bigger rocket or leave something behind.
Oxygen for only {0} days out of {1}. Give more power to life support: it makes oxygen from water.
Water for only {0} days, and the next ship comes in {1} (with reserve). Send the geologist to mine ice: it is much cheaper than water from Earth!
Food for only {0} days, but the next ship comes in {1} (with reserve). Take food boxes: food is hard to make on the Moon!
Mission goal: build a {0}. Pack {1} more kit(s), or bring building materials.
The oxygen tank holds only {0}. Extra oxygen will be wasted. Take something else!
Risky: {0}% chance to fail. Add a bit more fuel to be safe.
Great packing! The crew has everything for the mission. Press CONFIRM!
This module opens in a later chapter.
This module is not available yet. It opens in a later chapter.
Last until the next ship: {0} + {1} reserve
Why a reserve? If a ship has to turn back, it arrives later.
In real space, launch windows to the Moon open about once a month. In our game, time runs much faster!
With fuel the ship weighs like {0} elephants!
With fuel the ship weighs like {0} cars!
Reached the Moon on the first try
Enough supplies until the next ship, with a reserve
Nothing wasted: no extra oxygen, the rocket is not too big
Tip: take more food, water or oxygen, so the crew can wait for the next ship.
Tip: the oxygen tank holds only {0}. Extra oxygen is wasted.
Tip: the {0} rocket could carry this too, and it flies faster.
Tip: watch the traffic light. Green means a safe flight.
The ship is waiting! Send the order in a comms window.
First, fly the crew to the Moon.

NO LINK · the antenna has no power
The order is empty. Press PACK THE SHIP and choose the cargo!
Not enough fuel: the ship turned back and comes {0} late.
Sending cancelled. Now you can change the order.

We count only the ship that flies to the Moon: the capsule with the crew and the cargo. A real Moon rocket at launch weighs about 2,900 tonnes, like 600 elephants! Almost all of it is fuel, and its big stages fall off on the way.
A real Moon rocket weighs about 2,900 tonnes at launch, like 600 elephants! Only a small capsule reaches the Moon.
Launch pads stand by the ocean: used rocket parts fall into the water, far from people.
At launch, water pours under the rocket. It makes the roar quieter and protects the pad.
Parking orbit around Earth: checking all systems (about 1.5 laps)
Flying to the Moon: about 3 days, engines off
Moon orbit: braking with the engines
Landed! Welcome to the Moon's south pole.
Rockets are really built in Dnipro! The Zenit and Cyclone rockets and the first stage of the Antares rocket were made here.
In orbit, the ship flies around the whole Earth in about 90 minutes!
We aim not at the Moon, but where it WILL be in 3 days: the Moon keeps moving along its orbit (the dotted circle). The farther from Earth, the slower the ship: Earth's gravity pulls it back.
The Moon has no air, so parachutes don't work there. The ship slows down with its engines.
Dark craters at the Moon's south pole hide ice. That's water for our base!
Ships come often, but only the small Bee rocket: big rockets need more time to get ready for launch.
A ship now and then: the Bee or the Pelican.
Ships come rarely, but it can even be the heavy Whale. The wait is long, so take more supplies now!
The plan was chosen before the first launch.
This rocket is not in your supply plan. Choose a smaller one.
The supply plan is chosen before the first launch.
The cargo hold is full! Take something out first.
This cargo won't fit into this rocket's hold. Take something out first.
The storm is over! While you waited, some fuel boiled away. Check the traffic light again.
Clear sky: perfect weather for a launch. Only the fuel matters.
Strong wind pushes the rocket sideways. With extra fuel (green light) it's fine. On yellow, the risk gets bigger.
Thunderstorm! Lightning can hit a rocket, so real rockets never launch in a storm. You can wait, but the super-cold fuel slowly boils away.
There is no storm right now.
Thunderstorm at the launch site on Earth! The supply ship will start {0} hours later.
It was windy on Earth, but the supply ship took off.
On the way ({0}) the crew will eat {1} food and breathe {2} oxygen.
With the crew: {0} on the way. They will eat {1} food and breathe {2} oxygen. Water is cleaned and reused on board.
On the way the crew ate {0} food and breathed {1} oxygen.
Max Q: the air pushes hardest. Engines ease off a little.
Stage separation! The empty first stage falls away.
The rocket leans east and speeds up.
Engines off. We are in orbit!
ALARM! The engines stopped. The rescue system pulls the capsule away!
Empty fuel tanks are just extra weight. The rocket drops them, so flying gets easier.
Rockets lean east on purpose: the Earth spins that way and gives them a free push.
In orbit the ship flies about 28 000 km/h. That's 8 km every second!
Real crew ships have a rescue system: small motors pull the capsule away from the rocket, and parachutes bring the crew down safely.
Mission time: {0} d {1} h {2} min (sped up)
Moon orbit reached. Starting the descent!
Straight down: picking a flat spot without rocks
Contact! Engine off. We have landed!
The crew steps onto the Moon
Landing takes about 12 minutes. Parachutes need air, and the Moon has none, so the ship brakes with its engine.
At the south pole the Sun always stays near the horizon, so shadows are very long. Deep craters never see sunlight and keep ice inside.
There is no air on the Moon, so dust flies in straight lines and falls right away. No dust clouds!
On the Moon you weigh 6 times less. Astronauts don't walk, they hop!
Solar panels at the pole stand upright: the sunlight comes from the side, from just above the horizon.
The crew walks between the rooms inside: no spacesuit, no airlock, no radiation outside.
Tunnel ordered! Robots are on their way.
A tunnel can only go to the next square in the same row.
A tunnel joins only rooms: habitat, greenhouse, lab, medbay or shelter.
There is already a tunnel here.
Robots finished a tunnel! Now the crew walks between the modules without spacesuits.
There is no room in this row on this side yet. Build one: a tunnel can go across several empty squares.
A tunnel runs through this square, so you can't build here.
Something already stands between the rooms. A tunnel needs empty squares.
